quests.explanation: From Latin 'cras' (tomorrow), to procrastinate literally means to push something off until 'tomorrow.'
The prefix 'micro-' means 'very small,' so to micromanage means controlling even the smallest details of someone's work.
From Latin 'delegare' (to send), to delegate means to officially 'send' or assign a task to someone else.
The prefix 'ambi-' means 'both,' so feeling ambivalent means having 'both' (conflicting) feelings about something at once.
From Latin 'metus' (fear), 'meticulous' originally described someone fearfully careful — now simply extremely thorough and precise.
From Latin 'resilire' (to jump back), being resilient means having the ability to 'jump back' or recover quickly from difficulty.
From Latin 'tenere' (to hold), being tenacious means holding firmly onto a goal despite difficulty.
From Greek 'pragma' (deed or action), a pragmatic approach focuses on practical results rather than theory.
The suffix '-ive' turns the verb 'assert' (to state confidently) into an adjective describing someone confident and direct.
Sharing a root with 'diploma' (an official document), 'diplomatic' originally related to formal negotiations and now describes tactful behavior.
The prefix 'mal-' means 'bad,' so malware is simply 'bad' (harmful) software.

quests.hint: Remember it's spelled with 'ph,' like a play on 'fishing': PHI-SHING.
quests.explanation: This modern tech term deliberately mimics the spelling of 'fishing,' since scammers 'fish' for your personal information.
This compound word describes malicious software that holds your files for 'ransom' until you pay to release them.
When an adjective ends in '-able,' the noun form changes to '-ability,' the same pattern as 'scalable' to 'scalability.'
From Greek 'bios' (life) and 'metron' (measure), biometric security measures unique physical traits, like fingerprints.
From Latin 'expedire' (to free the feet), an expedition is a journey, often for exploration or a specific purpose.
Borrowed from French 'reconnaître' (to recognize), this word keeps a notoriously difficult double-letter pattern: 'nn' and 'ss.'
The suffix '-ary' turns 'expedition' into an adjective describing a force or group organized for a specific journey or mission.
The prefix 'un-' negates 'precedented' (having happened before), so unprecedented describes something never seen before.
Related to 'climate,' to acclimatize means to adjust your body to a new climate or environment, like high altitude.
From Greek 'a-' (without) and 'rhythmos' (rhythm), arrhythmia describes a heartbeat that has lost its normal, steady rhythm.
From Greek 'haima' (blood) and 'rhegnynai' (to burst), a hemorrhage is severe bleeding from a burst blood vessel.
From Latin 'suscitare' (to revive), to resuscitate means to bring someone back to life or consciousness 'again.'
The prefix 'de-' means 'remove,' so a defibrillator removes dangerous 'fibrillation' (irregular heartbeat) with an electric shock.
The prefix 'a-' means 'without,' so an asymptomatic illness shows 'without' any noticeable symptoms.
The suffix '-tic' turns 'cinema' into an adjective describing something visually striking, like in a film.
When a verb ends in '-ise' (or '-ize'), the noun form often becomes '-isation,' as in 'improvise' to 'improvisation.'
From Greek 'protos' (first) and 'agonistes' (actor/competitor), the protagonist is literally the 'first' or main character.

quests.hint: Compare with 'protagonist' — it's 'anti' plus 'agonist': ANTI + AGONIST.
quests.explanation: The prefix 'anti-' means 'against,' so an antagonist is the character who works 'against' the protagonist.

quests.hint: Tricky spelling: SO-LIL-O-QUY, ending in '-quy,' not '-key.'
quests.explanation: From Latin 'solus' (alone) and 'loqui' (to speak), a soliloquy is a speech a character gives while 'alone,' speaking their thoughts aloud.
